findings.title: 689,543 flow(s) report more payload bytes than wire bytes across 2 class(es); ddos materially affected
findings.detail: Payload bytes are a subset of the bytes that crossed the wire, so a flow where orig_bytes exceeds orig_ip_bytes (or resp_bytes exceeds resp_ip_bytes) is arithmetically impossible: Zeek derives the first from TCP sequence numbers, which wrap on scan and RST traffic, and counts the second off the wire, which cannot. These are the same columns that carry the largest label correlation in 2017 (point-biserial -0.442) and the largest attack-class mutual information (0.835), so the corruption sits exactly where the label signal is and every expectation or model built on it inherits the wrap. Use orig_ip_bytes and resp_ip_bytes instead.

findings.title: ddos/DNS misses 2 of 5 behavioural expectation(s), worst by 70.0%
findings.detail: The flows carrying this label do not behave the way the label names. Either the window is over the wrong traffic, or the band in expectations.yaml is wrong -- the measured rate and the floor it missed are both reported so the reader can tell which.

evidence.why: Every 2019 reflection vector rides UDP by construction. TCP here means the window caught something other than the reflected flood.
The victim is a sink, not a participant. Measured at 0.962 conn_state S0 across the whole 2019 ddos class.

evidence.sql: ("id.orig_p" IN (53, 123, 161, 1900, 389, 1434, 69, 137, 111) AND coalesce(orig_ip_bytes, 0) > 4 * coalesce(resp_ip_bytes, 0)) OR ("id.resp_p" IN (53, 123, 161, 1900, 389, 1434, 69, 137, 111) AND coalesce(resp_ip_bytes, 0) > 4 * coalesce(orig_ip_bytes, 0))
evidence.why: Amplification is a claim about direction, so it is tested on whichever side carries the amplifier's service port. Written both ways deliberately -- the 2019 captures are taken at the victim, where the reflector is the party that speaks first and the amplifier port lands in id.orig_p, but that is an inference from byte_ratio (median -3.04, i.e. the originator sends ~1000x what it receives) and not something the profile proves directly. PROVISIONAL.
PROVISIONAL. Reflected DNS responses carry port 53 on the reflector's side.
A flood converges on a target. 2019 puts 71.8M flows on two victim addresses.

findings.title: duration is null for 13.16% of ddos flows and 1 other class(es)
findings.detail: 9,489,180 flow(s) carry no duration. The EDA spec coalesces this feature's nulls to 0, so those flows are indistinguishable from flows that genuinely measured zero, and a class whose zero mass is really missing data will look flood-shaped whether or not it is. Nothing here says the labels are wrong -- it constrains which features a downstream claim about the affected classes may rest on, and requires that nulls be excluded explicitly rather than read as zeros.

findings.title: CICFlowMeter artefact probes ran over 72,533,839 flows and found none of the signatures
findings.detail: Reported because the negative result is the finding. Rosay et al. (ICISSP 2022) identified four artefact classes that CICFlowMeter writes into every CSV it generates -- constant bulk features from an integer division, ARP frames read as IPv4 traffic between 8.0.6.4 and 8.6.0.1, non-TCP/UDP packets collapsed to protocol 0 with ports 0, and TCP flows cut at the first FIN whose halves can end up labelled differently -- and stated that every dataset shipping CICFlowMeter CSVs carries them, CIC-IDS-2017, CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 and CIC-DDoS-2019 included. Talos does not use those CSVs; the lake is Zeek output over the original pcaps. This check is the measurement behind that claim, so that 'our features do not carry the published artefacts' is a reading rather than an assertion. Probe 1 has no literal equivalent in Zeek's schema and is reported as inapplicable rather than faked.

findings.title: 2 capture(s) were recorded on exactly the dates the manifest asserts
findings.detail: Recorded because this one is worth being able to point at. CIC-DDoS-2019's published calendar does not match its own capture clocks: the site presents the two days as January 12th and March 11th 2019, while the flows read 2018-12-01 and 2018-11-03. The folder names CSV-01-12 and CSV-03-11 are capture dates written DD-MM, which the website re-presents as MM-DD in 2019. Two independent confirmations: the FKIE COMIDDS catalogue quotes CSVs/CSV-03-11/Portmap.csv carrying Timestamp = 2018-11-03 10:01:35.983831, and CICFlowMeter issue #69 reports the site's 'January 12th' against pcap timestamps reading December 1st. Our manifest uses the capture dates, and the flows agree with it to the day. Had it used the published ones, every window would sit months away from the traffic and every rule would match zero flows while the pipeline reported success.
